slides.title: Reverse game theory
slides.body:
Standard game theory: given a game, find the equilibrium.

**Mechanism design**: given a desired outcome, design the rules so the equilibrium produces it.

The canonical question: how do you allocate a scarce resource among bidders with private valuations, in a way that's both **efficient** (item goes to who values it most) and **incentive-compatible** (bidders don't want to lie about their valuations)?

Mechanism design is mechanism design *before* equilibrium analysis — design the game so the equilibrium is what you want.

Applications:
- Online ad auctions (Google, Meta, Amazon).
- Spectrum auctions (FCC, Ofcom).
- Kidney exchange (algorithmic matching).
- School choice (NYC, Boston).
- AI alignment ([[principal-agent]]) — increasingly important.

slides.title: The setup
slides.body:
**Players**: $n$ agents, each with a private **type** $t_i$ (a valuation, cost, capability — known to themselves, not to others).

**Designer**: specifies a mechanism $(g, p)$:
- $g(\hat{t})$: an **allocation rule** — who gets what.
- $p(\hat{t})$: a **payment rule** — who pays what.

**Players** report types $\hat{t}_i$. They don't have to report truthfully — they'll report whatever maximizes their payoff.

**Designer** commits to executing $g(\hat{t})$ + $p(\hat{t})$ given the reports.

The mechanism is **truthful** (incentive-compatible) iff truth-telling is a dominant strategy for every player. If so, the designer can trust the reports.

question.question: Why is **truthfulness** the desirable property for a mechanism?
options: Truthfulness lets the designer reason about the mechanism's outcome without modeling each player's strategic deception — the designer can take reports at face value, and the equilibrium outcome equals the outcome under true types
Truthful mechanisms are always the most efficient
question.explanation: Truthful mechanisms collapse the strategic-modeling problem. Without truthfulness, the designer must reason about complex Bayesian Nash equilibria; with it, just take reports as given. Note: truthfulness does NOT imply efficiency or collusion-resistance — those are separate properties.

slides.title: The revelation principle
slides.body:
**Revelation principle (Myerson 1979)**: any social choice function implementable by *some* mechanism in Bayesian Nash equilibrium is also implementable by a *direct truthful* mechanism.

In plain English: if you want to design a mechanism producing outcome $X$ in equilibrium, you can WLOG restrict attention to mechanisms that simply ask each agent for their type and use it directly — making truth-telling the optimal strategy.

This collapses the design space. Instead of searching over all possible mechanisms × all equilibrium concepts, search over allocation rules + payment rules satisfying:
- **Incentive constraints**: truth-telling is best response.
- **Individual rationality**: participation is profitable.

Both are linear constraints; the optimization is solvable via standard techniques. The revelation principle is what makes mechanism design tractable as a mathematical theory.

slides.title: VCG: the canonical truthful mechanism
slides.body:
The **Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG)** mechanism is the canonical truthful mechanism for any allocation problem with quasi-linear utilities.

Each agent's payment = the **externality** they impose on others. Specifically: pay the difference between others' total surplus in this allocation vs others' surplus if you didn't exist.

**Single-item special case**: VCG = second-price auction. Bid your true valuation; if you win, pay the second-highest bid. Truthful by dominant strategy.

**Multi-item case**: more complex but the principle is the same. Online ad auctions descend from VCG.

**What VCG guarantees**:
- Truthful (dominant strategy).
- Efficient (item goes to highest-valuer).
- Individually rational (no losses).

**What VCG does NOT guarantee**:
- Revenue-optimal (Myerson's optimal auction is better).
- Collusion-resistant.
- Computationally tractable for combinatorial auctions (NP-hard winner determination).

question.question: Three bidders compete for a single item: A values it at 10, B at 7, C at 5. They bid truthfully in a Vickrey (second-price) auction. Who wins, and what do they pay?
options: A wins, pays 7 — winner pays the second-highest bid; truthful by dominant strategy because bidding above 10 risks paying more than valuation, bidding below risks losing when they'd profit
question.explanation: Vickrey: highest bidder wins, pays second-highest bid. A bids 10 and wins; pays B's bid of 7. Why is this truthful? Bidding above 10 doesn't help (you still win when you would've, and risk paying more than your valuation). Bidding below 10 doesn't help (you might lose to B at 7 — even though you'd profit). Truthful = dominant strategy.

slides.title: Connection to AI alignment
slides.body:
Mechanism design is the technical framework for thinking about **AI alignment**:

- **Reward model design** (RLHF) is mechanism design — design the reward so the trained policy's equilibrium matches human values.
- **Constitutional AI** is mechanism design — multi-principal mechanism with an internal AI auditor.
- **Mesa-optimization concerns** (Hubinger et al.) are principal-agent problems ([[principal-agent]]) — the trainer's 'agent' (the inner optimizer) has its own private information + may pursue its own objectives.

If you don't like what AI training produces, change the rules. That's mechanism design — applied to ML training procedures.

The intersection of mechanism design + AI safety is one of the most active areas of theoretical AI research in 2026.

Next: auction theory ([[auction-theory]]) — the most-deployed special case of mechanism design.

question.prompt: Why might 'truthful + efficient + individually rational' (i.e., VCG) NOT be sufficient for a real-world auction? Name at least two limitations.

rubricCriteria.description: Mentions that VCG isn't revenue-optimal — Myerson's mechanism does better
Mentions that VCG is vulnerable to collusion (bidder coalitions)

Mentions computational complexity for combinatorial auctions, OR mentions a third real-world limitation (collusion via coalitions, robustness to misspecified prior, complexity of explaining VCG to bidders)

slides.title: Revelation principle, in one paragraph
slides.body:
Suppose you have *any* mechanism that elicits useful information from agents with private types — say, a complex auction with strategic bidding.

The **revelation principle** (Myerson, Maskin): there's a direct mechanism with the same equilibrium outcomes where every agent's dominant strategy is to honestly report their type.

Consequence: when designing mechanisms, we can restrict attention to direct, truthful mechanisms WITHOUT loss of generality. The complexity of strategic behavior is absorbed into the mechanism's payment/allocation rule.

It's the most important meta-theorem in mechanism design: it reduces an infinite-dimensional search (over arbitrary mechanisms × agent strategies) to a finite-dimensional one (over direct truthful mechanisms).

VCG (Vickrey-Clarke-Groves): the canonical truthful mechanism for public-good provision and combinatorial auctions. Each agent pays the externality they impose on others. Strategy-proof, allocatively efficient (chooses the value-maximizing outcome). Limitations: budget-imbalanced, vulnerable to collusion, computational complexity in combinatorial domains. Still the standard reference point for any 'truthful mechanism' design.

question.question: VCG payments are computed as:
options: The minimum bid needed to win.
The externality each agent imposes on the others — the difference in others' total welfare with and without that agent.
question.explanation: VCG payments = externalities. Agent $i$ pays the difference $\max_x \sum_{j \neq i} v_j(x_{-i}) - \sum_{j \neq i} v_j(x)$ where $x_{-i}$ is the optimal choice without $i$ and $x$ is the chosen outcome. This pricing rule makes truthful reporting a dominant strategy and the mechanism allocatively efficient. Second-price auction is the single-item special case.

hints: VCG is built so the agent's incentive matches the social welfare impact of their decision.
The payment must align with each agent's contribution to the externality.
slides.workedSolution: VCG: agent $i$ pays the externality their participation imposes — the welfare loss to other agents from including agent $i$ in the optimization vs excluding them. Aligns individual incentive with social-welfare maximization, making truthful reporting dominant. Second-price auction is the single-item special case.

question.question: Mechanism design in the wild
question.prompt: Kidney exchange (Roth et al., Nobel 2012): patients with incompatible donors are matched in trades. Why is the truthful mechanism non-trivial here, and what role does the revelation principle play?
Explain in three sentences why mechanism design is 'reverse game theory'.
question.rubric: Mentions that mechanism design starts with the desired outcome (welfare-maximizing allocation) and engineers payoffs so equilibria deliver it; standard game theory takes rules as given and predicts equilibria; mechanism designers wear the rule-writer's hat.

objectives: Distinguish dominant-strategy from Bayesian incentive compatibility.
